chapter_theme: After worshipping the Jina, the king bows to a sage, and the sage, at the ministers' plea to turn away births, lists his topics, names the four states and the seven hells, and describes the first hell's pits and the sufferers who entered by their own deeds.

cast.role: King Payapati of Podanam, who turns to renunciation
the Lord the king worships, taken as the Jina
the sage of great austerity whom the king meets
the king's counsellors who ask the sage to turn away births
those born in the hell pits
the tormentors who crowd round the sufferers

1909.reading: The speaker says that when even Indra of the thousand red eyes comes and bows at the feet of the lord under the three white umbrellas, seeking his grace, then that lord's godhead is surely fitting.
1909.nuance: The verse does not name its speaker or the Lord; both are taken from the praise that closes at 1913, where the king bows to the Lord, so the speaker is the king by inference.

claims.claim: the Jina's lordship is such that Indra himself comes and bows at his feet

1910.reading: The speaker praises the Lord as one who has struck down fierce deeds, lit the lamp of true knowledge, walked on the lotus and sat on the golden seat and under the ashoka's shade, and asks whether the king of the gods will not come when so praised.
1910.nuance: The lotus, golden seat and ashoka tree are the stock marks of an arhat's court; the verse uses them as praise epithets, not as events.

claims.claim: the Jina destroyed fierce deeds and lit the lamp of true knowledge

1911.reading: The speaker tells the Lord that things that come to be and the three times lie inside his endless light of knowledge, and asks why he should be dazed by a world that is no different from himself.
1911.nuance: The last two lines are hard: the verse seems to ask what use there is in an all-knowing lord being dazzled by the world, but the sense of the vocative lines is not firm.

claims.claim: the Jina's endless knowledge holds all existing things and the three times

1912.reading: The speaker addresses the Lord as the holy king of dharma and says that bowing at his feet and begging him to remove their distress and light the dark world is a merit greater than any, since he has wholly conquered the two deeds.
1912.nuance: The two deeds (இருவினை) are read as good and bad deed; the verse does not say so.

claims.claim: the Jina has completely conquered the two kinds of deed

1913.reading: Having praised and bowed to the Lord, the king lays his head at the conqueror's feet, circles his shrine, and enters another golden pillared hall.
1913.nuance: The king is not named here; he is the subject carried over from the praise.
1913.event: The king worships the Jina, circles his shrine and enters the pillared platform hall.

1914.reading: In that hall sits a sage, firm like a great mountain with his many austere virtues, and the king wipes the dust from his lotus feet with the garland on his golden crown.
1914.nuance: The king's crown-garland becomes a cloth for the sage's feet: the ruler lowers the sign of his rank before an ascetic.
1914.event: The king touches the sage's feet with the tip of the garland on his crown.

1915.reading: The sage, whose great austerity has closed the springs that feed deeds and whose word is a mantra none can turn back, sits, and the king takes the seat that was fitting.
1915.nuance: ஊற்றுச் செறித்த is a Jain image of closing the channels of inflow (asrava); the verse has the word for springs only.
1915.event: The king takes the seat offered him before the sage.

claims.claim: austerity stops the springs from which deeds flow in

1916.reading: As the king sits bowed, the garlanded ministers say to the sage that he should feed them the nectar that ends torment and turn aside the tangled births so that they may be saved.
1916.nuance: The ministers ask for the teaching as a drink of nectar, so the plea is for relief from rebirth, not for advice on statecraft, which they could not give at 1857.
1916.event: The ministers ask the sage to feed them teaching that will turn away their births.

claims.claim: a sage's teaching can turn away the tangle of births

1917.reading: A speaker, with the king seated on his throne, remarks that the king who has had so much of the sweet wealth is asking about the holy greatness of dharma, and asks what it is that he is asking.
1917.nuance: Who asks and who answers is not fixed by the words: this is read as the king's turn to speak, but it could be the sage testing him.
1917.event: The king puts a question about dharma, or is questioned about it, before the sage.

1918.reading: The verse says of one who eats the food laid before him that he does not know how to bring his course to an end and does not mind its long-hated nature, and says the same of the handsome lord.
1918.nuance: The verse is obscure: it seems to describe a lord who enjoys his meals and has not learned how to end his round of births. The identification of the handsome lord with the king is a guess.

1919.reading: After the ministers have spoken, the king of austerity, whom the gods of the sky honour and whom the rule of his teaching has made great, begins to set out the matter for the king as if for Indra.
1919.nuance: The king is likened to Indra, as the sage is likened to a king of austerity: each is named in the other's terms.
1919.event: The sage begins his exposition for the king.

1920.reading: The great ascetic tells the lord to listen, and lists what he will tell: the states of rebirth, the deceit within them, the deed that fixes fate, the ways of conquering deeds, and the glory of the release the wise desire.
1920.nuance: This is a table of contents for what follows: hells, then (outside this chapter) the other states, then deeds and release.
1920.event: The sage sets out his five topics: rebirths, deeds and their conquest, and release.

1921.reading: The sage says that souls whirl like the turning cart wheel, the ring thrown by one without release and the drifting dust, and that there are four states they seek.
1921.nuance: Wheel, ring and dust are three pictures of the same turning: the soul has no fixed place and is moved by what it has done.
1921.event: The sage names four destinies that turn the souls.

claims.claim: souls whirl through four destinies as a wheel, a ring and dust turn

1922.reading: The sage names the four states as the hell-dwellers, the beasts, men and the good gods, and says an account of their kinds would grow long, so the king, whose heart melts, hears one way of telling it.
1922.nuance: The sage promises brevity here and then spends the rest of the chapter on the hells.
1922.event: The sage names the four states and says he will tell them briefly.

claims.claim: there are four states of birth: hell, animal, human and divine

1923.reading: The sage says the lower hells are cut into forty-nine layers, and that the dwellings of those who go to them number eighty-four lakhs.
1923.nuance: The numbers rest on a reading of ஏழாயிருபத்திரட்டியோடொன்பது as seven hells made of forty-nine layers; the verse gives only the numbers.
1923.event: The sage counts the layers and dwellings of the lower hells.

claims.claim: the lower hells have forty-nine layers and eighty-four lakh dwellings

1924.reading: The sage says the hells are named by what they are: darkness of darkness, darkness, smoke, merciless mire, sand, gravel and the bright stone, and the king should take each as its name says.
1924.nuance: The last of the seven, மணி, is read as the gem-stone of the first hell; the verse says only மருளின் மணி.
1924.event: The sage names the seven hells.

claims.claim: the seven hells are named for darkness, smoke, mire, sand and gravel

1925.reading: The sage says that the pain of those who have gone into the hells would make even the tellers shudder, and that he will give the words for the first of them.
1925.nuance: The sage says the telling itself would chill the speakers: the verse turns the description into a warning to a listener already uneasy.
1925.event: The sage begins to describe the first hell.

1926.reading: The sage says the first hell has thirteen levels with thirty lakh of dwellings, pits blazing with fire, and that there is no end to their number.
1926.event: The sage counts the pits of the first hell.

claims.claim: the first hell has thirteen levels and thirty lakh blazing pits

1927.reading: The pits are like chests split open, like cave mouths, like jars and pots, deep and wide with slippery mire, and are the place where wicked men are born.
1927.nuance: Birth, not arrival, is the word: the hell-dweller is born in the pit rather than sent to it.

claims.claim: the wicked are born in pits of mire in the hells

1928.reading: When the pits have taken shape and wailing bodies fill them, the beings slip onto burning rock and lie rolling, scorched and crumbled like worms.
1928.event: The pit-born beings fall on burning rock and writhe like worms.

1929.reading: Crumbled like worms they swell and rise, and after the smoke has risen they fall again and tumble in the same way, in a torment that never ceases for as long as their life lasts.
1929.nuance: The pain is endless only for the life-span there: the verse limits the torment to it, not to eternity.

claims.claim: hell torment does not pause for the whole span of life in hell

1930.reading: Those who cry 'alas, dharma' find no one who says 'we have come' and takes them out; burned and still not dying, they entered the pit through their own earlier striving in deeds.
1930.nuance: The cry is to dharma, not to a god, and no rescuer answers; the verse makes the cause the sufferers' own earlier striving, not a judge's decree.
1930.event: The sufferers cry out and no one answers, because their own earlier deeds sent them in.

claims.claim: those in hell entered it through their own earlier deeds and cannot be rescued

1931.reading: Some of cruel and licentious craft crowd around the sufferers and torment them, telling them to take in turn the many fruits of the deed they did before.
1931.nuance: The identity of the tormentors is not given beyond their trade; they are read as hell's attendants because they act on the sufferers.
1931.event: Hell's attendants torment the sufferers and tell them to take the fruit of their own earlier deeds.

claims.claim: the tormentors tell the sufferers they are receiving the fruit of earlier deeds

links.note: The ministers of 1916 ask the sage to turn aside the tangled births; 1920 lists what he will teach in answer.
links.teaches: The sage's list of topics shows that the answer to a plea for escape from births is first a map of the births themselves.

links.note: 1921 says four states turn the souls; 1922 names them as hell, beast, man and god.
links.teaches: The four are named at once, so the turning wheel is shown to carry a soul as easily into hell as into heaven.

links.note: 1844 says those who cut the root of good deeds will be kings in the hells; 1923 counts the layers and dwellings of those hells.
links.teaches: The hells of the earlier threat are shown to be a ranked place with room for every kind of fallen king.

links.note: 1923 counts the lower hells in all; 1926 narrows to the first and its thirteen levels and thirty lakh pits.
links.teaches: The sage's numbers are first given as a whole and then broken down hell by hell.

links.note: 1910 praises the Lord as one who has struck down fierce deeds and lit the lamp of knowledge; 2 hails him as light of the world who split fierce deeds.
links.teaches: The king's praise repeats the poet's opening praise, so the king's worship matches the epic's own account of the god.

links.note: 1921 turns the soul like a cart wheel through four states; Naladiyar 2 turns wealth like a cart wheel, never level with anyone.
links.teaches: The same cart wheel is used for what turns beneath a person in Naladiyar and for the person who is turned in the Soolamani.

gains.a: The wheel of 1921 gains a lesser double: the turning of wealth within one life as a small copy of the soul's turning through births.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a larger turning behind its wheel: wealth turns like a wheel because the one who holds it is turned by deeds from birth to birth.

links.note: 1930 says sufferers entered the pit by their own earlier striving and no one comes when they cry; Tirumanthiram 165 sends those who do not worship Siva to the seventh hell where they cry out.
links.teaches: The cry in hell is answered by neither text, but the Jain verse locates the cause in deeds and the Saiva verse in worship withheld.

gains.a: The cry of 1930 gains a Saiva counterpart in which a withheld act of worship, not a deed's weight, is the cause of the same crying.
gains.b: The Saiva hell gains a Jain rival in which no rescuer is named because no god sits above the deeds.

links.note: 1931 has tormentors tell sufferers to take the fruit of their own deeds; Tirumanthiram 198 has Death's servants bind killers and drive them with the very commands they gave.
links.teaches: Both hells have punishers who echo the victim's own deed, but only the Saiva servants act for Death, while the Soolamani's act for no one.

gains.a: The tormentors of 1931, named only by their trade, gain a Saiva figure to compare with: a servant who acts for Yama.
gains.b: The Saiva hell gains a Jain counterpart in which the punishers speak only of the deed the sufferer sowed.

links.note: 1931 has the sufferers receive the fruit of former deeds; Naladiyar 33 says the fool sighs hotly when the fruit arrives, and the wise who treat it as old debt pass beyond confusion.
links.teaches: 1931 shows the fruit received with no way to reinterpret it, which is the state Naladiyar 33 says the wise avoid.

gains.a: The hell scene gains the stance it lacks: the sufferers receive their deeds' fruit without the calm that frees.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a concrete picture of the fool it describes, shown in the pit rather than only named.

links.note: 1920 promises the way of conquering deeds as a thing the sage will teach; Tirumanthiram 219 says the fire worshipped burns up the many ills of deeds.
links.teaches: The Jain sage treats conquering deeds as a teaching to be given, while Tirumular treats it as a rite whose fire burns them.

gains.a: The sage's 'way of conquering deeds' gains a rival method, burning by rite, against which the Jain way can be read.
gains.b: The fire rite gains a Jain counterpart in which deeds are conquered by teaching and austerity, not by offering.

source_issues: 1909-1912 print as eight half-lines in the source; the tool joined them into four lines.
1917 and 1918 are obscure and their speakers are not fixed by the text.
